rationale: A wins because it has better proof discipline and fewer unsupported leaps. Its line, "a sample of the exported React/HTML-CSS so an engineer can judge quality," is exactly the right acid test for the strongest angle. B has real bones, but "a new product line with its own paid seat reads as evidence of the standalone path" asks a reporter to buy a strategy inference Figma has not put on the record.
gaps_in_A: "Figma's first move after the Adobe deal died" invents chronology. The update says the launch follows the Adobe collapse; it does not prove this is the first move.
"ship, not sell" is cute but loaded. It implies motive and strategic contrast the facts do not establish.
"category-creation" overclaims. Design-to-code/codegen already exists as a category; this is better framed as Figma moving deeper into it unless competitor context proves otherwise.
"shippable React code" risks outrunning the evidence. The fact says working front-end code; whether it is shippable is the proof question, not the headline.
gaps_in_B: "first big swing since the Adobe deal died is a bet on staying independent" stacks two unsupported claims: firstness and strategic intent.
"new product line with its own paid seat reads as evidence of the standalone path" turns pricing into corporate-strategy proof without an executive statement.
"funding-mechanics" is the wrong label for the pricing angle. This is SaaS monetization or AI add-on pricing, not funding mechanics.

"the handoff between designers and front-end engineers — a whole job boundary — is what's being automated" is a strong lens, but too absolute before code-quality proof. It may be scaffolding, not automation of a job boundary.
